professor.name: Dr. Reinholt
professor.text: Some philosophers contend that moral progress is real and measurable—citing the abolition of slavery or the expansion of rights—while others argue that what we call progress merely reflects the values of the present. Is moral progress a coherent idea? Defend your view.

students.name: Imogen
students.text: It is coherent. Certain changes, such as recognizing the suffering of excluded groups, are improvements by any reasonable standard, not just by our own.

students.name: Kwabena
students.text: Every generation believes its values are superior. Calling change 'progress' risks a kind of historical arrogance that future generations will judge just as harshly.

professor.name: Professor Langford
professor.text: Economists increasingly question whether GDP is an adequate measure of national success. Should governments replace GDP with broader indicators of wellbeing as their primary policy target? What would be gained and lost?

students.name: Sebastian
students.text: Yes. GDP counts environmental destruction and long working hours as gains, which systematically distorts policy priorities.

students.name: Aaliyah
students.text: Wellbeing indicators involve contestable value judgments; GDP's virtue is precisely that it is comparatively objective and hard to manipulate.

professor.name: Dr. Castellanos
professor.text: Some scholars argue that the concept of 'merit' in academic hiring is so shaped by networks and prestige that it largely reproduces existing hierarchies. Can merit be assessed fairly at all, and if so, how?

students.name: Lucia
students.text: Blind review of research and structured interviews can significantly reduce the role of prestige, even if they cannot eliminate it.

students.name: Henry
students.text: Merit is not an objective property waiting to be measured; it is defined by those already in power. Procedural fixes merely legitimize the outcome.

professor.name: Professor Osei
professor.text: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, some argue they should eventually be granted some form of legal personhood. Is this a meaningful proposal or a category error?

students.name: Theo
students.text: Legal personhood is a functional tool—corporations have it—so extending it to AI could clarify liability without implying consciousness.

students.name: Yasmin
students.text: Granting personhood would allow companies to shift responsibility onto their creations, which is precisely the wrong incentive.

professor.name: Dr. Adeyemi
professor.text: Some historians argue that individuals rarely change the course of history, which is shaped mainly by economic and social forces. Others emphasize the decisive role of particular leaders. Which view is more persuasive?

students.name: Rowan
students.text: Structural forces set the conditions, but at critical moments a single decision can redirect events, as many wartime examples show.

students.name: Mariam
students.text: Attributing change to great individuals is often a narrative convenience; the same pressures would have produced similar outcomes through someone else.

professor.name: Professor Valdés
professor.text: Is it legitimate for democracies to delegate significant decisions—on interest rates, for instance—to unelected expert bodies? Where should the boundary between technocracy and democracy lie?

students.name: Felix
students.text: Delegation protects long-term decisions from short-term electoral pressures, which ultimately serves citizens' interests.

students.name: Nadia
students.text: When major distributive consequences are decided by experts, citizens lose control over choices that are inherently political.

professor.name: Dr. Marsh
professor.text: Critics argue that 'effective altruism'—choosing charitable causes by calculating impact—neglects justice, community and the moral importance of proximity. Is impact-maximizing the right framework for giving?

students.name: Oskar
students.text: If we can save more lives elsewhere with the same money, partiality toward local causes is hard to justify morally.

students.name: Chiara
students.text: Reducing ethics to calculation ignores structural causes of poverty and the relationships that give moral obligations their force.

professor.name: Professor Thornbury
professor.text: Some legal scholars argue that the law should evolve to reflect changing social values, while others insist that legal stability and predictability are paramount. How should courts balance these demands?

students.name: Grace
students.text: Law that fails to adapt loses legitimacy; courts must interpret principles in light of contemporary understanding.

students.name: Viktor
students.text: When courts change the law, they usurp the role of legislatures; stability protects citizens from arbitrary judicial power.

professor.name: Dr. Halvorsen
professor.text: Does the widespread availability of information online make expertise less valuable, or more valuable than ever? Defend your view.

students.name: Lena
students.text: More valuable: the sheer volume of information makes the expert's ability to evaluate and synthesize it indispensable.

students.name: Jamal
students.text: Expertise is being democratized; informed amateurs now contribute meaningfully to fields once reserved for specialists.

professor.name: Professor Okwuosa
professor.text: Some argue that the climate crisis requires limiting individual freedoms, such as flying or meat consumption, through regulation. Others argue such limits are both unjust and politically self-defeating. Which position is more defensible?

students.name: Ingrid
students.text: Freedoms have always been limited to prevent harm to others; emissions harm future generations in ways that justify regulation.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: Restrictions on everyday choices provoke backlash that ultimately undermines climate policy; structural change in energy systems is the wiser path.

professor.name: Dr. Galloway
professor.text: Is the translation of literature fundamentally an act of interpretation that creates a new work, or can a translation be faithful to the original? What follows from your answer?

students.name: Sofia
students.text: Every translation is a new work; the translator's choices inevitably reshape tone, rhythm and meaning.

students.name: Daniel
students.text: Fidelity is a meaningful ideal even if never fully attained; otherwise we could not judge some translations better than others.

professor.name: Professor Achterberg
professor.text: Some cognitive scientists argue that free will is an illusion produced by unconscious processes. If true, what implications—if any—should this have for moral responsibility and criminal justice?

students.name: Hugo
students.text: If our choices are determined, retribution makes little sense; justice should focus on prevention and rehabilitation.

students.name: Amara
students.text: Responsibility is a social practice that remains meaningful regardless of metaphysics; abandoning it would undermine trust and cooperation.

professor.name: Dr. Lindqvist
professor.text: Universities have historically been sites of dissent. Has the increasing emphasis on student satisfaction and institutional reputation made them more cautious intellectually? Discuss.

students.name: Charlotte
students.text: Yes. When students are treated as consumers, institutions avoid controversy that might damage rankings or recruitment.

students.name: Rafael
students.text: Debate on campuses remains vigorous; what has changed is that more voices now participate, which some mistake for caution.

professor.name: Professor Reinholt
professor.text: Should future generations have legal representation—for example, through an ombudsman—in present-day policymaking? How could such representation work in practice?

students.name: Moana
students.text: An independent commissioner could review legislation for long-term impacts, as some countries already do with promising results.

students.name: Patrick
students.text: No one can know the interests of people not yet born; such institutions would simply amplify the preferences of their appointees.

professor.name: Dr. Thornbury
professor.text: In an era of deepfakes and synthetic media, is the evidential value of photographs and video permanently undermined? How should societies respond?

students.name: Kenji
students.text: Cryptographic authentication at the point of capture can restore trust in genuine recordings.

students.name: Elise
students.text: The deeper problem is social: people already believe what fits their views. Technical fixes cannot restore a shared sense of reality.

professor.name: Professor Marsh
professor.text: Some economists argue that inequality is not itself a problem as long as absolute poverty declines. Others hold that inequality has independent harms. Which view is better supported?

students.name: Tomasz
students.text: What matters morally is whether the worst-off are improving; focusing on inequality can lead to policies that make everyone poorer.

students.name: Priya
students.text: Extreme inequality corrodes democracy, as wealth translates into disproportionate political influence.

professor.name: Dr. Valdés
professor.text: Is the idea of a universal human rights framework compatible with cultural diversity, or does it impose particular cultural values globally?

students.name: Zainab
students.text: Core rights protect dignity in every culture; claims of cultural difference are often used by elites to justify oppression.

students.name: Lucas
students.text: The framework emerged from a specific tradition, and its application sometimes disregards legitimate differences in social organization.

professor.name: Professor Castellanos
professor.text: Should scientific research with potentially catastrophic misuse—such as certain gain-of-function studies—be restricted, even at the cost of slowing beneficial discoveries?

students.name: Isaac
students.text: Where the downside is catastrophic and irreversible, precaution must take priority over the speed of discovery.

students.name: Freya
students.text: Restrictions drive research into less transparent settings; open science with strict oversight is safer.

professor.name: Dr. Osei
professor.text: Is nostalgia a harmless sentiment, or can it be politically dangerous? Discuss with reference to contemporary examples.

students.name: Beatriz
students.text: Political appeals to a mythical golden age can justify exclusion and resistance to necessary reform.

students.name: Ethan
students.text: Nostalgia also preserves valuable traditions and expresses legitimate grief over lost communities.

professor.name: Professor Adeyemi
professor.text: Some argue that the attention economy—platforms optimized for engagement—poses a threat to human autonomy comparable to environmental harms. Is this analogy persuasive?

students.name: Noor
students.text: Yes. Like pollution, the harms are diffuse, cumulative and borne by individuals who never consented.

students.name: Callum
students.text: The analogy exaggerates; users retain choices in ways that people breathing polluted air do not.

professor.name: Dr. Langford
professor.text: Should literary works with offensive content from earlier eras be edited for modern readers, or should they be preserved intact? Defend your position.

students.name: Olivia
students.text: Altering texts erases historical evidence and disrespects authors; contextual introductions are the appropriate response.

students.name: Arjun
students.text: Children's books in particular may justifiably be revised, since their purpose is to be read, not studied.

professor.name: Professor Halvorsen
professor.text: Is the pursuit of scientific knowledge intrinsically valuable, or must it be justified by its benefits to society? Explain the implications of your view for research funding.

students.name: Lars
students.text: Knowledge has intrinsic value; many transformative applications emerged from research that seemed useless at the time.

students.name: Amina
students.text: Public funds are limited, so research must be prioritized by expected social benefit.

professor.name: Dr. Okwuosa
professor.text: Some political theorists argue for sortition—selecting legislators by lottery—as a remedy for the failings of electoral democracy. Is this a serious alternative?

students.name: Hana
students.text: Randomly selected assemblies are more representative and less susceptible to donors and party machines.

students.name: Jakob
students.text: Without electoral accountability, randomly chosen citizens could be easily steered by expert advisers and bureaucrats.

professor.name: Professor Galloway
professor.text: Do professions such as law and medicine have obligations to society that go beyond their obligations to individual clients and patients?

students.name: Diana
students.text: Yes. Professionals enjoy privileges granted by society, which entail duties such as stewardship of public resources.

students.name: Samuel
students.text: Undivided loyalty to the client or patient is the foundation of professional trust; competing social duties would erode it.

professor.name: Dr. Achterberg
professor.text: Is the concept of 'authenticity' in tourism—seeking 'real' local experiences—meaningful, or is it itself a product of the tourism industry?

students.name: Iris
students.text: The search for authenticity often turns local life into a performance staged for visitors.

students.name: Mateo
students.text: Meaningful encounters remain possible; the problem is commodification, not the aspiration itself.

professor.name: Professor Lindqvist
professor.text: Some argue that the growth of English as a global academic language has impoverished scholarship in other languages. Should this trend be resisted?

students.name: Pierre
students.text: Yes. Concepts embedded in other languages are lost, and scholars who write in English gain unfair advantages.

students.name: Mei
students.text: A common language has enabled unprecedented collaboration; resisting it would fragment the scholarly community.

professor.name: Dr. Reinholt
professor.text: To what extent should an individual's past online statements affect their present opportunities, such as employment or public office?

students.name: Laila
students.text: People change; permanent digital records create a punitive culture with no room for growth.

students.name: Oscar
students.text: For public office, past statements are legitimate evidence of character, though context and time must be weighed.

professor.name: Professor Thornbury
professor.text: Are markets the most effective way to allocate scarce resources such as organs for transplantation, or are some goods properly outside the market?

students.name: Felipe
students.text: Regulated compensation for donors could save thousands of lives that the current system loses.

students.name: Sana
students.text: Markets in organs would exploit the poor and corrupt the altruistic basis of donation.

professor.name: Dr. Marsh
professor.text: Is irony and satire an effective form of political criticism, or does it encourage cynicism and disengagement?

students.name: Rhys
students.text: Satire exposes hypocrisy in ways that earnest argument cannot, and it reaches audiences who avoid serious news.

students.name: Elena
students.text: Constant mockery breeds a sense that nothing can change, which benefits those already in power.

professor.name: Professor Valdés
professor.text: Should central banks consider climate risks and inequality when setting monetary policy, or should they confine themselves to price stability?

students.name: Benjamin
students.text: Climate risks threaten financial stability, so considering them falls within central banks' existing mandates.

students.name: Aiko
students.text: Expanding mandates politicizes central banks and undermines the independence that makes them effective.

professor.name: Dr. Castellanos
professor.text: Some argue that peer-reviewed journals should be replaced by open platforms where research is published immediately and evaluated afterwards. Would this improve science?

students.name: Anders
students.text: Post-publication review would accelerate discovery and expose flawed work to many more critics.

students.name: Ruth
students.text: Without gatekeeping, the volume of low-quality work would overwhelm readers, and the public would struggle to tell reliable findings from noise.

professor.name: Professor Osei
professor.text: Is it possible to separate the moral character of an artist from the value of their work? Should it matter to audiences?

students.name: Clara
students.text: The work stands independently; judging art by its creator's life impoverishes our cultural heritage.

students.name: Kofi
students.text: When we consume the work, we often enrich and honor the artist, so their conduct is morally relevant.

professor.name: Dr. Adeyemi
professor.text: Is the pursuit of energy self-sufficiency by individual nations compatible with an efficient global response to climate change?

students.name: Stefan
students.text: Self-sufficiency based on renewables enhances security and accelerates decarbonization simultaneously.

students.name: Yuki
students.text: Integrated international grids are far more efficient; national self-sufficiency duplicates investment and raises costs.

professor.name: Professor Langford
professor.text: Some argue that the emphasis on measurable outcomes in public services—targets, rankings, metrics—has undermined professional judgment. Is this critique justified?

students.name: Thomas
students.text: Yes. Professionals increasingly optimize for the metric rather than the purpose it was meant to serve.

students.name: Leah
students.text: Without measurement, poor performance remains hidden; the solution is better metrics, not abandoning them.

professor.name: Dr. Halvorsen
professor.text: Should wealthy societies pursue radical life extension through medical technology? Consider the social and ethical consequences.

students.name: Viktor
students.text: Extending healthy life is a continuation of medicine's purpose; there is no principled point at which to stop.

students.name: Amira
students.text: It would deepen inequality, strain resources and slow generational renewal of ideas and institutions.

professor.name: Professor Okwuosa
professor.text: Is national identity a necessary foundation for social solidarity and the welfare state, or can solidarity rest on other bases?

students.name: Jonah
students.text: Willingness to share resources historically depended on a sense of common belonging, which national identity provides.

students.name: Nia
students.text: Solidarity can rest on shared citizenship and mutual dependence, without requiring cultural homogeneity.

professor.name: Dr. Galloway
professor.text: Should autonomous weapons systems capable of selecting targets without human intervention be banned under international law?

students.name: Hassan
students.text: Delegating life-and-death decisions to machines crosses a fundamental moral line and removes accountability.

students.name: Freya
students.text: A ban is unenforceable; regulation requiring meaningful human control is more realistic.

professor.name: Professor Achterberg
professor.text: Does the digitization of archives and libraries democratize knowledge, or does it create new forms of exclusion and loss?

students.name: Wei
students.text: Digitization gives millions access to materials previously available only to a privileged few.

students.name: Marta
students.text: Choices about what to digitize reproduce existing biases, and digital formats risk becoming obsolete.

professor.name: Dr. Lindqvist
professor.text: Some argue that work will cease to be central to human identity in an automated future. Is this desirable, and how should societies prepare?

students.name: Gabriel
students.text: Liberation from compulsory labor could allow people to pursue more meaningful activities.

students.name: Ines
students.text: Work provides structure, purpose and social connection that leisure cannot easily replace.

professor.name: Professor Reinholt
professor.text: Is civil disobedience justified in a democracy when legal channels for change are available? Under what conditions?

students.name: Rosa
students.text: When legal channels are too slow to prevent serious harm, nonviolent disobedience can be a legitimate democratic act.

students.name: Erik
students.text: In a functioning democracy, breaking the law undermines the very procedures that protect minorities.

professor.name: Dr. Thornbury
professor.text: Should social scientists conduct research that might produce findings harmful to vulnerable groups, even if the findings are accurate?

students.name: Matthias
students.text: Suppressing accurate findings undermines science and ultimately harms those it claims to protect.

students.name: Adaeze
students.text: Researchers bear responsibility for foreseeable misuse and must consider how findings will be framed and used.

professor.name: Professor Marsh
professor.text: Is the concept of 'sustainable development' coherent, or does it attempt to reconcile goals that are fundamentally in tension?

students.name: Lina
students.text: It is coherent: development can be redefined around wellbeing rather than material throughput.

students.name: Paul
students.text: The phrase obscures real trade-offs and allows governments to avoid difficult choices.

professor.name: Dr. Valdés
professor.text: Do international rankings of universities serve students well, or do they distort the priorities of higher education?

students.name: Chloe
students.text: Rankings provide useful comparative information, especially for international students choosing between unfamiliar institutions.

students.name: Rahul
students.text: Rankings reward research output and reputation, pushing universities to neglect teaching quality.

professor.name: Professor Castellanos
professor.text: Should the use of genetic information by insurers be prohibited entirely, or are there circumstances in which it is fair?

students.name: Simone
students.text: Genetic risk is not chosen; penalizing people for it is a form of discrimination that must be prohibited.

students.name: Andreas
students.text: If applicants can use genetic information and insurers cannot, the asymmetry may make insurance markets unsustainable.

professor.name: Dr. Osei
professor.text: Is cultural appropriation a meaningful ethical concern, or does all culture develop through borrowing?

students.name: Aisha
students.text: Borrowing becomes harmful when dominant groups profit from the cultural forms of marginalized groups without acknowledgment.

students.name: Lukas
students.text: Policing cultural exchange stifles creativity; all traditions are hybrids of earlier borrowing.

professor.name: Professor Adeyemi
professor.text: Some argue that open borders would substantially increase global prosperity. Should this economic argument outweigh concerns about social cohesion?

students.name: Tara
students.text: The potential gains for the world's poorest are enormous and morally decisive.

students.name: Henrik
students.text: Rapid large-scale migration could undermine the institutions that create prosperity in the first place.

professor.name: Dr. Langford
professor.text: Should the teaching of philosophy be compulsory in secondary schools? What would it contribute that other subjects do not?

students.name: Imran
students.text: Philosophy teaches students to examine assumptions and reason carefully about values, which no other subject does explicitly.

students.name: Clara
students.text: Critical thinking can and should be cultivated within existing subjects rather than through an abstract additional course.

professor.name: Professor Halvorsen
professor.text: Is privacy best understood as an individual right or as a collective good? What difference does the framing make for regulation?

students.name: Oliver
students.text: Framing privacy as collective explains why individual consent is inadequate: my data reveals information about others.

students.name: Sana
students.text: Individual rights remain essential; collective framings risk subordinating persons to group interests.

professor.name: Dr. Okwuosa
professor.text: To what extent should museums and historical sites present uncomfortable aspects of national history to visitors?

students.name: Maya
students.text: Fully. A nation that cannot confront its past honestly cannot build a shared future.

students.name: Robert
students.text: Balance is needed; sites also serve to foster belonging, which a purely critical narrative may undermine.

professor.name: Professor Galloway
professor.text: Can there be such a thing as a 'just war' in the modern world? Evaluate the relevance of traditional just war theory today.

students.name: Felix
students.text: The principles of proportionality and discrimination remain indispensable for judging the conduct of contemporary conflicts.

students.name: Yara
students.text: Modern weapons and asymmetric conflicts make the theory's distinctions between combatants and civilians almost impossible to apply.
